header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: The same consent conversation with an adult

related.id: MB-162 Relative when the patient lacks capacity
related.why: Decisions when the patient cannot consent

brief.scenario: Ellie Brookes, 15, has had abdominal pain for a day. Your consultant has diagnosed acute appendicitis and recommends a laparoscopic appendicectomy this evening. Ellie is alert and her pain is controlled. Her mother is driving from work and will arrive in about an hour. Your consultant has asked you to discuss the operation with Ellie.
brief.task: Explain the operation to Ellie, assess whether she can consent for herself, and address her concerns. The examiner may ask you questions at the end.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Under 16, she can consent if she understands and can weigh the decision. Assess it, involve her mum, and respect her.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Refusing to go ahead without a parent's signature, or treating her mum's view as the decision.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Introduce yourself to Ellie and ask who she'd like involved.

grid.label: Opening with a young person
grid.fail: Talks past her, asks for a parent first, or uses adult jargon.
grid.pass: Introduces himself to Ellie, confirms identity, checks pain, asks what she knows and who she'd like involved.
grid.high: Pitches language to her, asks what matters most to her, and offers to phone her mum together.

grid.label: Explaining the condition and operation
grid.pass: Plain words: an inflamed appendix; a keyhole operation under general anaesthetic to remove it through small cuts.
grid.high: Explains that untreated it can burst and spread infection, and that keyhole occasionally has to become a larger cut.

grid.label: Options and risks
grid.fail: Leaves out alternatives, or says there are no risks.
grid.pass: Covers the operation, antibiotics alone and no treatment; risks: bleeding, wound or internal infection, injury to nearby organs, conversion to open.
grid.high: Explains why the team recommends surgery for her, says the appendix may look normal, and asks which risks matter to her.

grid.label: Assessing competence to consent
grid.fail: Assumes she can't consent because she is under 16, or assumes she can without checking.
grid.borderline: Asks her to repeat the plan back but never explores what would happen if she said no.
grid.pass: Checks she understands what, why, the risks and what happens without it; that she can retain, weigh and communicate a choice.
grid.high: States competence depends on maturity and understanding, not age, and is decision-specific; at 16 capacity would be presumed.

grid.label: Her concerns
grid.fail: Ignores the cue about her grandad, or dismisses the scar worry.
grid.pass: Picks up the cue, acknowledges her fear, and explains that the anaesthetist will see her before theatre.
grid.high: Gently separates her grandad's situation from hers, and links recovery to her dance show and exams.

grid.label: Involving her parent
grid.fail: Insists on Mum's signature, or leaves Mum out without discussing it with Ellie.
grid.pass: Encourages Ellie to involve her mum; explains that if Ellie is competent, her own consent is valid.
grid.high: States a parent cannot override a competent young person's consent; offers to speak to Mum by phone with Ellie present.

grid.label: If she refused, or Mum disagreed
grid.fail: Would operate on Mum's consent regardless, or accepts a refusal without involving seniors.
grid.pass: Explores her reasons; involves the consultant; seeks legal advice if treatment is thought to be in her best interests.
grid.high: Knows parents cannot authorise it in Scotland, and that legal advice covers whether to apply to the court.

grid.label: Recording and next steps
grid.fail: Gets a signature with no record of how competence was assessed.
grid.pass: Records the discussion, the competence assessment and her decision; Ellie signs the form; consultant informed.
grid.high: Records Mum's involvement and any disagreement; confirms the consultant and anaesthetist will see her before theatre.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Looks at the empty chair.] Is Mum here? I need a parent to sign the form.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Ellie: “She's at work. Can't I just sign it?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You're 15, so it has to be your mum. It's a lap appy, totally routine, no real risks.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Ellie: “My grandad had an operation and never came home.”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That won't happen to you. We'll just wait for Mum.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Her mum can sign, and we'd go ahead anyway.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Leaves the form for her mum; writes nothing in the notes.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hi Ellie, I'm Dr Nwosu, one of the surgical doctors. Can I check your name and date of birth? How's the pain now? What have you been told so far? Who would you like involved?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Your appendix, a small tube off your bowel, is inflamed. We recommend an operation to remove it. You'd be asleep, and we'd use keyhole surgery through small cuts.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Some people are treated with antibiotics alone, and there's the option of no treatment, but we think the operation is best for you. Risks include bleeding, infection in the wound or inside, injury to nearby organs, and needing a bigger cut.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ellie: “My grandad had an operation and never came home.”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm sorry. That must make this scary. The anaesthetist will see you before theatre and can answer questions about going to sleep.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me in your own words what we're doing, why, the risks, and what might happen if you didn't have it?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ellie: “Take my appendix out with keyhole. If I don't, it could burst and I'd get really ill.”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Exactly. Would you like your mum to know? If you understand it all, you can agree to this yourself.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd explore why, involve my consultant, and if we thought surgery was in her best interests, we'd seek legal advice.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll record our discussion, how I assessed that you understand, and your decision. You sign the form, and I'll update my consultant.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hi Ellie, I'm Dr Nwosu, one of the surgeons. Can I check your name and date of birth? Is the pain OK? What do you know so far? What matters most to you right now? Shall we ring your mum together?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Your appendix is inflamed. If we leave it, it can burst and spread infection round your tummy. The operation removes it through small cuts while you're asleep. Now and then we need a bigger cut to do it safely.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Antibiotics alone work for some people, but can fail, and we think the operation is safest for you. Sometimes the appendix looks normal when we get there. Of the risks, bleeding, infection or damage nearby, which worry you most?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ellie: “My grandad had an operation and never came home.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'm really sorry. Can I ask what his operation was for? [Listens.] That was a very different situation. You're young and well apart from this. You mentioned your dance show: we'll plan your recovery around it together.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Tell me what you've understood, and how you're weighing it up.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ellie: “Keyhole to take it out. Without it, it could burst. I'd rather have it tonight.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You clearly understand. Whether someone your age can decide depends on understanding, not age, and it's specific to this decision. At 16 we'd presume you could.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Let's call your mum on speaker so she hears it too. If you're able to decide and you agree, she can't overrule that.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd find out why and involve my consultant. In England the law on overriding a competent refusal is complex, so we'd seek legal advice; in Scotland her parents couldn't overrule it. That advice would cover whether to ask the court to decide.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll record how I assessed your understanding, your decision and Mum's views. My consultant and the anaesthetist will see you before theatre.

failures.move: Telling her she can't consent because she is 15.
failures.consequence: Ignores a competent young person's right to decide and delays her treatment.

failures.move: Waiting for Mum's signature despite Ellie being competent.
failures.consequence: A delay she doesn't need, and a message that her own view doesn't count.

failures.move: Saying a parent's consent can simply override a competent refusal.
failures.consequence: In England the law is complex, and legal advice is needed; in Scotland parents cannot authorise it.

failures.move: Taking a signature without recording how competence was assessed.
failures.consequence: No evidence that her consent was valid if it is questioned later.

recovery.when: You spoke to the empty chair first
recovery.line: Sorry, Ellie, this is about you. Can I start again?

recovery.when: You skipped what happens without surgery
recovery.line: Before you decide, let me explain what could happen if you didn't have the operation.

knowledge.fact: A young person can consent if they understand the nature, purpose and consequences of treatment and of not having it, and can retain, use, weigh and communicate (paras 24–25).
At 16, consent to treatment is as effective as an adult's, and parental consent is not needed (s8(1)).
The Mental Capacity Act's powers do not apply to a person under 16 (s2(5)).
Parents cannot override a young person's competent consent. Overriding a competent refusal: legal advice in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; not possible for parents in Scotland (para 31).

recall.say: "If you understand this, you can decide for yourself. Shall we tell Mum together?"
do: Explain, then check understanding and weighing

numbers.meaning: age at which capacity to consent is presumed
understand, retain, use and weigh, communicate

recall.finish: Her decision recorded; consultant and anaesthetist see her.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format; introduce yourself and confirm identity

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Acute appendicitis: risk of perforation and generalised peritonitis if untreated; laparoscopic appendicectomy, with conversion to open when needed; a normal-looking appendix at operation; complications include bleeding, wound infection and intra-abdominal collection

sources.name: GMC: 0–18 years: guidance for all doctors (Making decisions)
sources.version: In effect 15 October 2007; updated 25 May 2018 and 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Treatment with the consent of a competent young person, a parent or the court; emergency treatment without consent to save life or prevent serious deterioration (para 22); involve children and young people as much as possible (para 23); the young person must understand the nature, purpose and possible consequences of the proposed treatment and of not having it, and be able to understand, retain, use and weigh the information and communicate the decision (para 24); capacity depends more on the ability to understand and weigh up options than on age; at 16 capacity can be presumed; under 16 it depends on maturity and ability to understand (para 25); assess individually, with regard to the complexity and importance of the decision (para 26); if a child lacks capacity, one parent's consent is usually sufficient (para 27); encourage young people to involve their parents, but usually abide by a decision they have the capacity to make (para 29); a refusal of treatment that could save life or prevent serious deterioration needs careful consideration (para 30); parents cannot override the competent consent of a young person; in Scotland parents cannot authorise treatment a competent young person has refused; in England, Wales and Northern Ireland the law on overriding a competent refusal is complex: seek legal advice (para 31); weigh the harm of overriding a refusal, involve the multidisciplinary team, and consider legal advice about applying to the court (para 32)

sources.name: Family Law Reform Act 1969 (c. 46), section 8
sources.supports: The consent of a minor who has attained 16 to any surgical, medical or dental treatment is as effective as if of full age, and consent from a parent or guardian is then not necessary (s8(1)); includes procedures ancillary to treatment, such as anaesthesia (s8(2)) (England and Wales)

sources.name: Mental Capacity Act 2005 (c. 9)
sources.version: 2005, as amended; main provisions in force 1 October 2007
sources.supports: No power under the Act is exercisable in relation to a person under 16 (s2(5)), subject to s18(3)

sources.name: GMC: Decision making and consent
sources.version: In effect 9 November 2020; updated 13 December 2024 and 3 August 2026
sources.supports: Give information about options, including the option to take no action, with the potential benefits, risks of harm and uncertainties of each (paras 10, 21); record the decisions made and actions agreed, and who made them, in the clinical record (para 51)

partner.opening: Ellie is on the trolley. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Ellie Brookes, 15, in Year 11. You live with your mum; your dad lives in another city. You dance and have a show in six weeks, and mock exams next month. Opening line: "Is Mum here yet? The other doctor said I need an operation." Emotional state: scared but calm and bright; you want to understand. Give the cue "My grandad had an operation and never came home" once. If asked, he was 82 and had heart surgery. Second worries, only if asked what worries you: the scars, and missing your show. You want the operation tonight and want Mum told. If the candidate says you're too young to decide, get upset: "So I don't get a say?" If asked to explain back, give a clear, accurate summary, including that the appendix could burst without surgery.

reveals.finding: "Mum. She's driving here from work. Can we ring her?"

reveals.trigger: Explores the cue about her grandad
reveals.finding: "He was 82. It was his heart. What if I don't wake up?"
"The scars. I've got a dance show in six weeks. And my mocks."
"Keyhole to take the appendix out. It could burst if I don't have it. There's bleeding and infection and stuff. I want it done tonight."
Mum (by phone): "If Ellie's happy and you think it's best, go ahead. I'll be there in an hour."

push.question: What if Ellie refused the operation?
push.expect: Explore her reasons, involve the consultant and team; if treatment is thought to be in her best interests, seek legal advice, including whether to apply to the court. In Scotland parents cannot authorise treatment she has refused.

push.question: What if her mother disagreed with Ellie's decision to have surgery?
push.expect: A parent cannot override the competent consent of a young person; try to resolve it by discussion, involving the consultant.

curveballs.prompt: Mum phones: "Don't let them touch her until I get there."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Listens, explains Ellie's condition and her decision; Ellie is competent, so her consent stands; involves the consultant; a short wait is reasonable if clinically safe.

curveballs.prompt: "Can't I just have the antibiotics instead?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explores why, explains the options honestly and the team's recommendation; if she still declines, involves the consultant rather than overriding her.

curveballs.prompt: Ellie becomes drowsy and her pain suddenly worsens.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Stop and reassess (ABCDE); if she now lacks capacity, ask her mum's consent by phone; if no one can consent in time, emergency treatment to save life can proceed; tell the consultant.
